In a B2B travel platform the expensive bugs don't look like bugs. A refund that pays out twice returns HTTP 200. So does a fare the client sets to one rupee, or an agency reading another agency's passports. Scanners look for bad inputs. We built Paradox, which looks for impossible outcomes.

Here is a real finding. Book, pay, cancel, cancel again. Every response is 200 OK, and the agency's wallet grows by 7,776 rupees each time. Paradox learns the platform from what TBO already gives teams: recorded traffic, gateway logs and test accounts, with no API docs. It replays real journeys with one thing changed and checks twelve rules every correct platform obeys. The agency's balance never grows from its own actions. The same booking never costs less. One agency's data never reaches another. It plants canary data in everything it creates, so leaks are proven by the canary, and it measures every money bug in rupees. A finding exists only when a rule breaks and the proof repeats three times.

It already works. Across randomised test runs with bugs it had never seen, Paradox found every one with zero false alarms, while a signature scanner on the same inputs found under a third and none of the money or cross-agency bugs. On an airline platform it was not built for, it found five of seven at first contact and seven of seven after two general fixes. It uses exactly TBO's stated inputs, tests new deploys first, closes fixed tickets itself, and is safe by construction: scope allowlist, only its own test data, rate limits with back-off, a kill switch and a full audit log.
